title: Outer ear infection
intro: Outer ear infection, or otitis externa, is inflammation of the skin of the ear canal, often called swimmer's ear. It causes pain, itching and sometimes discharge. It is usually treated with ear drops and clears within a week or two. Keeping the canal dry and not poking it help prevent it.

sections.heading: Causes
paragraphs: The skin lining the ear canal is normally protected by a thin waxy layer. Water that stays in the ear, cotton buds, hearing aids, earplugs, eczema and scratching can break this barrier, allowing bacteria or sometimes fungi to grow. Swimming, humid weather and narrow canals raise the risk.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: Typical signs are ear pain that worsens when the outer ear is pulled or pressed, itching, redness, a feeling of fullness, muffled hearing and clear or yellowish discharge. Fever is unusual. The pain can be intense and disturb sleep.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: A doctor examines the ear canal and often cleans it carefully. Antibiotic or antiseptic drops, sometimes combined with a mild steroid, are used for about a week. If the canal is swollen shut, a small wick may be inserted to carry the drops. Painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen ease discomfort. Fungal infections need antifungal drops.
Keep the ear dry during treatment, and do not use cotton buds or objects. Stop swimming until the doctor says it is fine.

sections.heading: Prevention
paragraphs: Dry the ears gently after swimming or showering, tilting the head and using a towel on the outside only. Avoid cleaning inside the canal, use earplugs for swimming if you are prone to infections and clean hearing aids as advised. Treat underlying eczema.

sections.heading: When to seek help
paragraphs: See a doctor promptly if pain is severe, there is facial swelling, fever, hearing loss, dizziness or if you have diabetes or weakened immunity, since a rare severe form can spread to bone. Seek advice if symptoms do not improve after a few days of treatment.

examples.title: After swimming
examples.text: Imagine your ear aches the day after a holiday in the sea. You could avoid cotton buds, see your doctor and use the prescribed drops exactly as directed.

examples.title: Preventing recurrence
examples.text: Suppose you have had this several times. You might ask whether earplugs or drying drops would help, and avoid inserting anything into your ears.
